examples.title: Understand your own play
examples.lede: Not “you won 61%” — which deck, which mode, which week, and whether the grind is actually paying off.

examples.title: Pick your next deck
examples.lede: What is winning in the recorded corpus, weighted by results rather than by how often you see it on a stream — with the sample sizes attached.

examples.title: Push with evidence
examples.lede: Trophy pushes stall for boring, findable reasons. A record of every battle makes the pattern visible instead of anecdotal.

examples.title: Follow your friends
examples.lede: The people you play with, tracked because you asked — what they are on, how much they are playing, and what changed since you last looked.

examples.title: Win your river race
examples.lede: The finished race, the one that just opened, and who has battled so far today — from a record the game's own API forgets after twenty weeks.

examples.title: Keep the roster healthy
examples.lede: Who has gone quiet, who just arrived, and who the game itself has stopped counting — so a check-in happens before a race is lost.

examples.title: Scout the other clan
examples.lede: Every race captures all five clans in the bracket, and a curated collection keeps the clans you care about recorded — so the comparison is always there to ask for.

examples.title: Write the weekly recap
examples.lede: The numbers are already recorded; the writing is the only work. Your agent drafts it and you paste it into clan chat.

examples.title: Answer your clanmates
examples.lede: An agent acts for one clan rather than for you: its own door, its own key, its own feed — and a map from a Discord id to a player tag.

examples.title: Publish your own stats
examples.lede: Build a clan site or a bot on the record instead of on a second Clash key. Pull at build time; no scraping, no push.

examples.title: Run a collector
examples.lede: Volunteer a machine that fetches for the corpus. It is named for a card, credited to you, and it raises what Elixir records for you.
